1. Core Clinical Tension: A 28-year-old previously healthy male presents with a fulminant multiorgan failure syndrome characterized by jaundice, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, ecchymoses, and life-threatening pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage requiring invasive mechanical ventilation. While rodent exposure immediately brings rat-bite fever to mind, the syndrome of severe icterohemorrhagic multiorgan involvement (Weil's syndrome) represents severe leptospiral vasculitis, which can be misattributed to fulminant sepsis with DIC, hantavirus infection, or autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndromes.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint is set at the patient's transfer and initial triage in the medical ICU—including the history of the rat bite 10 days prior, exam showing jaundice and ecchymosis, mechanical ventilation parameters, initial triage labs (neutrophilic leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal transaminases, elevated BUN and creatinine, non-proteinuric urinalysis), and chest CT revealing diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities consistent with alveolar hemorrhage—prior to confirmatory serological/microbiological verification and later hospital course complications.
3. Differential Distinctions: Rat-bite fever (Streptobacillus moniliformis) follows rodent bites but manifests with migratory polyarthritis and maculopapular rash rather than profound icterohemorrhagic Weil's syndrome. Hantavirus infections (HFRS/HCPS) feature rodent exposure, renal failure, and pulmonary edema/hemorrhage, but typically show heavy proteinuria and lack cholestatic jaundice with normal transaminases. Sepsis with DIC presents with coagulopathy and shock, whereas leptospirosis characteristically produces marked hyperbilirubinemia out of proportion to aminotransferases alongside pulmonary capillaritis and renal tubular damage.
case_prompt:
A 28-year-old previously healthy male presented in respiratory failure and multiorgan decompensation after an acute febrile illness. Ten days prior to admission, he sustained a rat bite to his left big toe, for which he received a tetanus vaccination and wound assessment at an outpatient facility. Several days later, he developed progressive constitutional symptoms including headache, generalized weakness, and severe diffuse myalgias. He subsequently noted high fevers, generalized yellow discoloration of the skin and sclerae, and rapidly worsening shortness of breath. His respiratory status deteriorated rapidly, necessitating endotracheal intubation and transfer to the intensive care unit.

On physical examination upon ICU arrival, he was sedated on synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation (PEEP 10 cmH2O, FiO2 1.0, pressure support 20 cmH2O, set respiratory rate 18 breaths/min). He was markedly pale and deeply jaundiced. Cutaneous examination revealed ecchymoses over the upper and lower extremities. Auscultation of the chest revealed bilateral basal crackles. Vital signs demonstrated a temperature of 38.6°C, heart rate of 88 beats per minute, blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 99% on 100% FiO2.

Arterial blood gas analysis on admission showed a pH of 7.40, PaCO2 of 45.3 mmHg, and HCO3 of 28 mEq/L. Complete blood count revealed marked leukocytosis with neutrophilic predominance, normocytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Serum chemistries demonstrated markedly elevated blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine consistent with acute kidney injury. Liver function testing revealed severe conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with relatively normal aminotransferase levels. Urinalysis was notable for the absence of proteinuria. A non-contrast computed tomography scan of the chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral patchy alveolar infiltrates and ground-glass opacities consistent with alveolar hemorrhage.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the direct history of a rat bite to the left foot 10 days earlier. However, rat-bite fever characteristically manifests with migratory polyarthralgias, asymmetrical joint effusions, and an acral pustular or maculopapular exanthem, rather than the severe icterohemorrhagic triad of severe conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, acute renal failure, and diffuse pulmonary capillaritis with alveolar hemorrhage.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Ten days before admission, the patient had a rat bite in his left big toe, so he sought medical advice, where he was given a tetanus vaccine and discharged with a recommendation to follow up at the infectious clinic.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to rodent exposure leading to acute renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates/hemorrhage. Ruled out because hantavirus infections typically cause massive proteinuria and hemoconcentration without the profound cholestatic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal transaminases observed in this patient.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The transaminases level was average. There was a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine levels were significantly increased, suggesting acute renal injury. Urine analysis showed no proteinuria.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Fulminant Sepsis with Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered in any patient presenting with high fever, ecchymoses, thrombocytopenia, pulmonary infiltrates, and multi-organ dysfunction. Ruled out as the primary etiology by the disproportionate cholestasis with preserved transaminases, specific rodent bite history, and prominent pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage indicative of infectious capillaritis rather than pure consumable coagulopathy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: CT scan showed diffuse bilateral areas of patchy alveolar infiltration ground glass opacities, representing alveolar hemorrhage

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot was the constellation of rat exposure followed by classic Weil's syndrome (jaundice, acute kidney injury, and severe pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage with thrombocytopenia), definitively confirmed by targeted diagnostic testing.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: So, he was admitted to the medical ward in Gaza, where Investigations were performed and confirmed the diagnosis of leptospirosis. Those revealed alveolar hemorrhage, cholestatic jaundice, and acute kidney injury.

editor_comments: Admission breakpoint placed at initial ICU triage with baseline labs and chest CT findings. Zero disease or pathogen spoilers in case_prompt. Verbatim quotes from case text verify differential rule-outs and diagnostic pivot. Target canonical disease Leptospirosis verified.
